title: MoAlign: Motion-Centric Representation Alignment for Video Diffusion Models
claim: Generative models violate real-world dynamics in a concrete failure case; aligning internal features with motion-specific features from a pretrained encoder fixes it.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right; left failure/fix video rows, right pipeline diagram
description: A two-panel figure with dashed rounded borders. The left panel opens with the text prompt "A coin falls into a cup". Two rows of four video frames follow. The top row, labeled CogVideoX-2B, shows a coin hovering upright above a cup, captioned "Physics law violated: The coin keeps floating in air". The bottom row, labeled MoAlign-2B, shows a bitcoin-like coin falling into the cup across frames, captioned "Physics law maintained". The eye goes first to these large photo-like frames. The right panel is a small pipeline. A real video of a cat on grass goes into a frozen VideoMAE encoder (snowflake icon), then a Motion Projection block, then a grid of blue motion-specific feature tiles. A dashed double-headed arrow labeled Feature Alignment links these tiles to a Diffusion Model box with a fire icon, which is fed the prompt "A cat walks slowly on the ground". The panel is captioned "Model tuning to align with real motion".
caption: Problem (Left): Physics laws are often violated in outputs of video diffusion models. Base CogVideoX model (top) cannot generate a coin falling into a cup: the coin floats in the air instead. Our MoAlign method (bottom) improves this. Proposed solution (Right): Our finetuning pipeline aligns internal representations of the diffusion model with motion-specific features extracted from VideoMAEv2.
abstract: Text-to-video diffusion models have enabled high-quality video synthesis, yet often fail to generate temporally coherent and physically plausible motion. A key reason is the models' insufficient understanding of complex motions that natural videos often entail. Recent works tackle this problem by aligning diffusion model features with those from pretrained video encoders. However, these encoders mix video appearance and dynamics into entangled features, limiting the benefit of such alignment. In this paper, we propose a motion-centric alignment framework that learns a disentangled motion subspace from a pretrained video encoder. This subspace is optimized to predict ground-truth optical flow, ensuring it captures true motion dynamics. We then align the latent features of a text-to-video diffusion model to this new subspace, enabling the generative model to internalize motion knowledge and generate more plausible videos. Our method improves the physical commonsense in a state-of-the-art video diffusion model, while preserving adherence to textual prompts, as evidenced by empirical evaluations on VideoPhy, VideoPhy2, VBench, and VBench-2.0, along with a user study.
